meta.title: The Request on the Last Line
meta.skill_frame: Argument and evidence: find the claim when it arrives at the end of the text.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.39, 5.50 and 5.91 on the three parts (102, 103 and 100 words), 5.60 together. The load is a claim that arrives after two pages of setup, so the reader has to hold the problem and know which sentence asks for anything.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for argument_evidence 4.1, band 4.1, sequence 4. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A repair shop memo that describes a storm week, the parts counter and the free shelf space before it asks for monthly ordering of common parts.
source.avoided: No shop name, street, or price. No claim about how many parts the shop sells.

session.difficulty_basis: The claim sits in the last sentence after two pages of situation, so a reader who stops early has the setup and not the request.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: For years the repair shop on the corner ordered parts one job at a time. A worker wrote the order when a bike came in and then waited for the box to arrive. Most boxes came within three days, which was fast enough for most jobs and kept the rack clear. Two winters ago a storm closed the road for a week and stopped the trucks, and twelve bikes waited on the rack with nothing to fix them. The shop lost that week, and it could not promise the owners a date. The owner still has the list of those twelve bikes.
passage.part_2: The memo describes that week, then the parts counter, then the shelf space the shop now has free. It ends with one sentence, and the sentence asks for a change. The shop should order the ten most common parts once a month, so a box is always on the shelf. That sentence is the claim. Everything before it is the situation that makes the claim worth considering. The memo takes its time getting there, and the early pages are easy to mistake for the point of the whole document. A reader has to reach the last line to find what the shop wants.
passage.part_3: Reading the memo backward helps, because the last sentence carries the request. The earlier pages describe the problem the change would solve and the room it would use. A reader who stops after the second page has read the setup and missed the claim. A summary that says the memo is about a storm has missed it too. The end of the memo is where the shop stops describing and starts asking. The claim is the request, and the pages before it are the reason the request is on the table. Nothing in the first two pages asks for anything.

items.prompt: What happened to the shop two winters ago?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. A storm closed the road, and twelve bikes waited a week.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says a storm closed the road for a week and twelve bikes waited on the rack with nothing to fix them.
tutor_only.tell: A storm shut the road for a week, and twelve bikes sat on the rack waiting.
help: The sentence about the storm carries the answer.
It names a number of bikes and a number of days.
accept_ideas: a storm closed the road
twelve bikes waited a week
the road shut for a week
a storm stopped the trucks
not_required: what the bikes cost to repair
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the shop closed for good
if_they_say.ask: The shop lost a week. What stopped the trucks?

tutor_only.full_idea: A storm closed the road for a week, and twelve bikes waited.

items.prompt: What does the memo ask the shop to change?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Order the ten most common parts once a month.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The last sentence says the shop should order the ten most common parts once a month and keep them on the shelf.
tutor_only.tell: The memo asks the shop to order the ten most common parts once a month. It wants them kept on the shelf.
help: The sentence that starts with 'The shop should order' carries the request.
It names a number of parts and a month.
tutor_only.core_idea: Order the ten most common parts once a month and keep them on the shelf.
accept_ideas: order the ten common parts once a month
keep the common parts on the shelf
order common parts monthly
stock the ten most common parts
not_required: which parts are the most common
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the shop should close
if_they_say.ask: The memo asks for one change in ordering. What does it name?

items.prompt: Which sentence in the memo is the claim?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The last sentence, the one that asks for the change.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the memo ends with one sentence that asks for a change, and that sentence is the claim.
tutor_only.tell: The claim is the last sentence, where the shop is told to order common parts once a month.
help: The sentence about the end of the memo names what the claim is.
It tells where the memo stops describing.
tutor_only.core_idea: The last sentence, which asks the shop to order common parts once a month.
accept_ideas: the last sentence
the sentence about ordering parts monthly
the one asking for monthly orders
the final line of the memo
not_required: how many pages the memo runs
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the sentence about the storm is the claim
if_they_say.ask: The storm is described, not asked for. Which sentence asks for a change?

items.prompt: A reader says the memo is about the storm. Why is that not the claim?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The storm is the situation, and the claim is the request at the end.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the earlier pages describe the problem the change would solve, and the claim is the request in the last sentence.
tutor_only.tell: The storm explains why the change is worth considering. The claim is the request that comes at the end.
help: The sentence about the claim and the pages before it carries the answer.
Separate the problem from the request.
tutor_only.core_idea: The storm is the situation that makes the change worth considering, and the claim is the request.
accept_ideas: the storm is the problem, not the request
the claim is the request at the end
the pages before describe the problem
the storm makes the request worth considering
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says both are claims
if_they_say.ask: One sentence asks for something. Which one?

tutor_only.full_idea: The storm is the situation that makes the change worth considering, and the claim is the request.

items.prompt: Why does the memo describe the parts counter and the free shelf space before it asks for anything?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. They show the problem and the room the change would use.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the earlier pages describe the problem the change would solve and the room it would use.
tutor_only.tell: The pages show what went wrong and where the parts would go, which is the reason for the request.
help: The sentence about what the earlier pages describe carries the answer.
Look at what the memo does with the two pages.
tutor_only.core_idea: They show the problem the change would solve and the room it would use.
accept_ideas: to show the problem and the free space
to give the reason for the request
they set up the request
